src.explanation: Angiotensin-converting enzyme levels are elevated in 40 to 80% of patients with sarcoidosis. Other laboratory findings include leukopenia, eosinophilia, an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, hypercalcemia in about 5% of patients and hypercalciuria.

src.explanation: Methotrexate is one of the immunosuppressants most commonly used when sarcoidosis is corticosteroid-intolerant or refractory, and it treats many autoimmune diseases such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis. It is also implicated as a cause of interstitial lung disease in the drug list and the treatment-related box.

cites: Inflammatory Lung Disease 2026.pptx, Slides 22, 65

src.question: Which interstitial lung disease can produce an episodic presentation?
src.explanation: An episodic presentation is less common in interstitial lung disease and can be seen with hypersensitivity pneumonitis, where inhaled organic material leads to illness after exposure, and symptoms can be reversible if the problem is caught early.

items.section_title: 3.3 · Laboratory tests, imaging and pulmonary function
items.html: Reticular opacities on the chest film. Among reticular opacities, fine ground-glass change is an early finding and medium reticular change, honeycombing, is a late finding. Moving from ground glass to honeycombing marks progression, consistent with fibrosis, which damages the alveoli permanently.
cites: Inflammatory Lung Disease 2026.pptx, Slides 5, 26

src.question: A 61-year-old woman with interstitial lung disease had a chest film 5 years ago showing fine reticular, ground-glass opacities. Her new film shows medium reticular opacities described as honeycombing. How should this change be classified?
src.key: Progression from early to late disease
src.explanation: Among reticular opacities, fine ground-glass change is an early finding and medium reticular change, honeycombing, is a late finding. Moving from ground glass to honeycombing over 5 years marks progression, consistent with fibrosis, which damages the alveoli permanently.

items.html: Onset patterns. Interstitial lung disease can present acutely over days to weeks, subacutely over weeks to months, chronically over months to years, or episodically. The episodic pattern of recurrent bouts is less common and can be seen with hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
cites: Inflammatory Lung Disease 2026.pptx, Slide 22

src.question: A 44-year-old man has had four separate bouts of cough and dyspnea over the past year, each clearing completely between bouts. Which onset pattern of interstitial lung disease does his course fit?
src.explanation: Interstitial lung disease can present acutely over days to weeks, subacutely over weeks to months, chronically over months to years, or episodically. The episodic pattern of recurrent bouts is less common and can be seen with hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which makes his exposures worth reviewing.

items.section_title: 3.1 · Interstitial lung disease: what it is and what causes it
items.html: Drug-induced interstitial lung disease. Nitrofurantoin is one of the treatment-related causes of interstitial lung disease, beside radiation, methotrexate, amiodarone and chemotherapeutics, and it is also named among drugs that cause pulmonary toxicity. Exertional dyspnea, dry cough, crackles and restriction after years of use fit a drug cause.
cites: Inflammatory Lung Disease 2026.pptx, Slides 12, 23, 24, 35, 40, 72

src.question: A 66-year-old woman has taken nitrofurantoin for years to prevent recurrent urinary tract infections. Over several months she has developed progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry cough, with bibasilar inspiratory crackles and a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing. She has no occupational, bird or mold exposures. What is the most likely cause of her interstitial lung disease?
src.explanation: Nitrofurantoin is one of the treatment-related causes of interstitial lung disease, beside radiation, methotrexate, amiodarone and chemotherapeutics, and it is also named among drugs that cause pulmonary toxicity. Years of use followed by exertional dyspnea, dry cough, crackles and restriction fit a drug cause.

items.section_title: 3.1 · Interstitial lung disease: what it is and what causes it
items.html: Occupational and environmental exposures. Exposures are grouped as inorganic dusts, organic dusts and fumes or gases. Stone work releases free crystalline silica, and pneumoconiosis is caused by inhaled coal dust or various inorganic or silicate dusts, so stone work is an inorganic dust exposure.
cites: Inflammatory Lung Disease 2026.pptx, Slides 12, 13, 50, 60, 65

src.question: A 52-year-old man has spent 20 years cutting and polishing stone in a quarry. He now has progressive exertional dyspnea and a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing. How is his occupational exposure classified?
src.explanation: Occupational and environmental exposures are grouped as inorganic dusts, organic dusts and fumes or gases. Stone work releases free crystalline silica, and pneumoconiosis is caused by inhaled coal dust or various inorganic or silicate dusts, so his exposure is an inorganic dust.

items.html: Lupus pernio. Lupus pernio, skin sores on the face, is the skin involvement of sarcoidosis. A dry cough, insidious dyspnea, nontender lymphadenopathy and liver and spleen enlargement complete its multi-organ picture. Sarcoidosis also occurs more often in Black patients and in women.
cites: Inflammatory Lung Disease 2026.pptx, Slides 18, 25, 35, 39, 40, 42, 43

src.question: A 38-year-old Black woman has a dry cough and dyspnea of insidious onset. She has lupus pernio (skin sores on the face), nontender lymphadenopathy and liver and spleen enlargement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.explanation: Lupus pernio, skin sores on the face, is the skin involvement of sarcoidosis, and a dry cough, insidious dyspnea, nontender lymphadenopathy and liver and spleen enlargement complete its multi-organ picture. Sarcoidosis also occurs more often in Black patients and in women.

items.html: Advanced disease. Right heart failure appears with advanced interstitial lung disease, and dyspnea that has spread from exertion to rest also marks progression. Early in the disease the examination may be normal.
cites: Inflammatory Lung Disease 2026.pptx, Slides 22, 23, 24, 73

src.question: A 76-year-old man has had interstitial lung disease for 9 years, and his dyspnea now occurs at rest. An echocardiogram shows right heart failure. What does the right heart failure indicate about his lung disease?
src.key: It is at an advanced stage
src.explanation: Right heart failure appears with advanced interstitial lung disease, and dyspnea that has spread from exertion to rest also marks progression. Early in the disease the examination may be normal, so these findings place him late in a long, chronic course.

items.html: Silicosis presentation. Sandblasting is a free crystalline silica exposure, and silicosis shows silicotic nodules 1-10 mm across throughout the lungs with eggshell calcification of the periphery of the hilar lymph nodes. Dyspnea, cough, weight loss, fatigue and crackles fit its presentation.
cites: Inflammatory Lung Disease 2026.pptx, Slides 26, 44, 58, 60, 61, 63, 69

src.question: A 48-year-old man has worked as a sandblaster for 20 years. He has dyspnea, cough, weight loss and fatigue with crackles on examination. His chest film shows nodular opacities, 1-10 mm across, throughout both lungs, and eggshell calcification of the periphery of the hilar lymph nodes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.explanation: Sandblasting is a free crystalline silica exposure, and silicosis shows silicotic nodules 1-10 mm across throughout the lungs with eggshell calcification of the periphery of the hilar lymph nodes. Dyspnea, cough, weight loss, fatigue and crackles fit its presentation.

items.html: Methotrexate to avoid. Methotrexate is one of the immunosuppressants used for corticosteroid-refractory sarcoidosis, but it has also been implicated as a cause of interstitial lung disease. Azathioprine or infliximab covers the same refractory indication, so methotrexate should be avoided in a patient whose lung injury it already implicated.
cites: Inflammatory Lung Disease 2026.pptx, Slides 12, 18, 46, 47

src.question: A 47-year-old man with cardiac sarcoidosis has corticosteroid-refractory disease. He also has rheumatoid arthritis, and methotrexate he once took for it was stopped after it was implicated in lung injury. His team is weighing methotrexate, azathioprine, infliximab and continued corticosteroids. Which of these should be avoided?
src.explanation: Methotrexate is one of the immunosuppressants used for corticosteroid-refractory sarcoidosis, but it has also been implicated as a cause of interstitial lung disease, and in him it already was. Azathioprine or infliximab covers the same refractory indication without that history.

items.section_title: 3.3 · Laboratory tests, imaging and pulmonary function
items.html: Restrictive pattern on testing. Interstitial lung disease stiffens the lung so it no longer expands, giving a restrictive pattern: total lung capacity and forced vital capacity fall while the ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity stays normal or rises.
cites: Inflammatory Lung Disease 2026.pptx, Slides 4, 23, 24, 26, 29

src.question: A 58-year-old woman has 8 months of progressive exertional dyspnea and a persistent nonproductive cough, with bibasilar dry rales and small lung volumes on examination. Which combination of total lung capacity and ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity is expected?
src.key: Low capacity, normal or high ratio
src.explanation: Interstitial lung disease stiffens the lung so it no longer expands, giving a restrictive pattern: total lung capacity and forced vital capacity fall while the ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity stays normal or rises. Her small lung volumes on examination fit.

items.html: Complications of silicosis. The complications of silicosis are an increased risk of tuberculosis, progressive massive fibrosis and scleroderma. Scleroderma is also one of the connective tissue diseases that produce interstitial lung disease.
cites: Inflammatory Lung Disease 2026.pptx, Slides 18, 25, 64

src.question: A 50-year-old woman who has cut and polished stone for 22 years has silicosis. Her clinician reviews the known complications of silicosis, one of which is a connective tissue disease. Which connective tissue disease is it?
src.explanation: The complications of silicosis are an increased risk of tuberculosis, progressive massive fibrosis and scleroderma. Scleroderma is also one of the connective tissue diseases that produce interstitial lung disease, so new findings in her deserve that thought.

items.section_title: 3.3 · Laboratory tests, imaging and pulmonary function
items.html: Restrictive pattern. A restrictive pattern is a normal or increased ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity (normal 0.70 or more) with decreased total lung capacity and forced vital capacity (normal 80% or more of predicted).
cites: Inflammatory Lung Disease 2026.pptx, Slides 26, 29, 34

src.question: A 63-year-old woman with exertional dyspnea and bibasilar crackles has pulmonary function testing: forced vital capacity 58% of predicted (normal 80% or more), total lung capacity 61% of predicted (normal 80% or more), and a ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity of 0.86 (normal 0.70 or more). How is this pattern classified?
src.explanation: A restrictive pattern is a normal or increased ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity with decreased total lung capacity and forced vital capacity. Her ratio of 0.86 is preserved while both capacities sit near 60% of predicted, the pattern interstitial lung disease produces.

items.html: Recovery after acute respiratory distress syndrome. Long-term recovery includes treating physical sequelae: post-intensive care muscle wasting, weakness and persistent fatigue. Rehabilitation addresses them while lung function continues to improve over 6 to 12 months.
cites: Inflammatory Lung Disease 2026.pptx, Slides 48, 54, 71, 74

src.question: A 66-year-old man is recovering after 3 weeks in the intensive care unit for acute respiratory distress syndrome. He has muscle wasting, weakness and persistent fatigue. Which referral addresses these problems?
src.explanation: Long-term recovery after acute respiratory distress syndrome includes treating physical sequelae: post-intensive care muscle wasting, weakness and persistent fatigue. Rehabilitation addresses them while his lung function continues to improve over 6 to 12 months.

items.html: Corticosteroids in sarcoidosis. Hypercalcemia (calcium above the 8.5-10.5 mg/dL range) is one of the indications for oral corticosteroids in sarcoidosis. About 90% of cases respond to corticosteroids, so they come first even when the chest film shows hilar adenopathy alone.
cites: Inflammatory Lung Disease 2026.pptx, Slides 44, 46, 47, 48, 71

src.question: A 38-year-old woman with biopsy-proven sarcoidosis has bilateral hilar adenopathy alone on chest film and no eye, heart or nervous system involvement. Her serum calcium is 11.9 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5). Which treatment is indicated?
src.explanation: Her calcium of 11.9 mg/dL is above the 8.5-10.5 range, and hypercalcemia is one of the indications for oral corticosteroids in sarcoidosis. About 90% of cases respond to corticosteroids, so they come first even when the chest film shows hilar adenopathy alone.

items.html: Management of coal workers' pneumoconiosis. Management is supportive, with oxygen, vaccinations, rehabilitation and smoking cessation, and in severe cases lung transplant may be indicated.
cites: Inflammatory Lung Disease 2026.pptx, Slides 48, 54, 74

src.question: A 56-year-old coal miner has severe complicated coal workers' pneumoconiosis with worsening dyspnea despite oxygen, vaccinations, pulmonary rehabilitation and smoking cessation. Which referral may be indicated?
src.explanation: Management of coal workers' pneumoconiosis is supportive, with oxygen, vaccinations, rehabilitation and smoking cessation, and in severe cases lung transplant may be indicated. He has severe disease that is worsening despite every supportive measure on the list.

items.section_title: 1.7 · The four waveforms of a normal EEG
items.html: What shapes the electroencephalogram. The intensity and patterns of electrical activity on the electroencephalogram are determined by the level of excitation of different parts of the brain, which varies with sleep, wakefulness and brain disorders such as epilepsy or psychosis.
cites: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 10, 21, 28

src.question: What determines the intensity and pattern of electrical activity on the electroencephalogram?
src.explanation: The intensity and patterns of electrical activity on the electroencephalogram are determined by the level of excitation of different parts of the brain, which varies with sleep, wakefulness and brain disorders such as epilepsy or psychosis.

items.section_title: 1.6 · The cycle between sleep and wakefulness
items.html: What ends wakefulness. After the brain has remained active for many hours, neurons in the activating system become fatigued. The positive feedback cycle between the mesencephalic reticular nuclei and the cerebral cortex fades, and the sleep-promoting centers take over.
cites: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 14, 18, 19

src.question: In the proposed theory, what ends a long period of wakefulness?
src.explanation: After the brain has remained active for many hours, neurons in the activating system become fatigued. The positive feedback cycle between the mesencephalic reticular nuclei and the cerebral cortex fades, and the sleep-promoting centers take over.

items.section_title: 1.5 · Why sleep matters: the physiological functions
items.html: Sleep restriction. Sleep restriction over a few days can decrease a person's cognitive and physical performance, overall productivity and health. That is one reason sleep is considered essential, even though its specific physiological functions are still being researched.
cites: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 9, 16, 17

src.question: Which outcome follows sleep restriction over a few days?
src.explanation: Sleep restriction over a few days can decrease a person's cognitive and physical performance, overall productivity and health. That is one reason sleep is considered essential, even though its specific physiological functions are still being researched.

items.html: Electrooculogram. The electrooculogram, the eye-movement recording, shows the irregular, sharply peaked eye movements of rapid eye movement sleep. The eye muscles are spared from the atonia that affects other voluntary muscles, so the eyes keep moving.
cites: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 10, 12, 28

src.question: Which recording shows the irregular, sharply peaked eye movements of rapid eye movement sleep?
src.explanation: The electrooculogram, the eye-movement recording, shows the irregular, sharply peaked eye movements of rapid eye movement sleep. The eye muscles are spared from the atonia that affects other voluntary muscles, so the eyes keep moving.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Slow-wave (non-rapid eye movement) sleep, and the comparison
items.html: Stage N3. Stage N3, also called deep sleep, is restful sleep and the deepest non-rapid eye movement stage, marked by delta waves. Body and tissue growth and repair occur in it, and it decreases with age.
cites: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 6, 9, 28

src.question: Which stage is the deepest sleep of the night?
src.explanation: Stage N3, also called deep sleep, is restful sleep and the deepest non-rapid eye movement stage, marked by delta waves. Body and tissue growth and repair occur in it, and it decreases with age.

items.html: Rapid eye movement episodes when sleepy. When a person is extremely sleepy, each rapid eye movement episode is short or even absent. As the person becomes more restful and less sleepy, the duration of rapid eye movement episodes increases, so the later periods of a night are longer.
cites: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 7, 9

src.question: Which circumstance makes rapid eye movement episodes short or even absent?
src.explanation: When a person is extremely sleepy, each rapid eye movement episode is short or even absent. As the person becomes more restful and less sleepy, the duration of rapid eye movement episodes increases, so the later periods of a night are longer.

items.html: Electromyogram. The electromyogram, the muscle recording, shows atonia of voluntary muscles in rapid eye movement sleep, sparing the eye muscles and diaphragm, as inactivity due to inhibited alpha motor neurons.
cites: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 12, 28

src.question: Which recording shows the atonia of voluntary muscles during rapid eye movement sleep?
src.explanation: The electromyogram, the muscle recording, shows atonia of voluntary muscles in rapid eye movement sleep, sparing the eye muscles and diaphragm, as inactivity due to inhibited alpha motor neurons.

items.section_title: 1.8 · EEG changes across wakefulness and sleep
items.html: Delta waves. Waves slower than 3.5 cycles per second with high voltage are delta waves, and delta waves mark stage N3, the deep, restful and deepest non-rapid eye movement stage, in which body and tissue growth and repair occur.
cites: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 25, 26, 27, 28

src.question: During sleep, the electroencephalogram shows high-voltage waves slower than 3.5 cycles per second. Which stage fits?
src.explanation: Waves slower than 3.5 cycles per second with high voltage are delta waves, and delta waves mark stage N3, the deep, restful and deepest non-rapid eye movement stage, in which body and tissue growth and repair occur.

items.html: Coma versus sleep. Arousability separates the two states: sleep is unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by sensory or other stimuli, and coma is unconsciousness from which a person cannot be aroused. Failure to rouse to any stimulus points to coma.
cites: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 5, 10, 12, 14, 26, 28

src.question: In an unconscious person, which observation points to coma rather than sleep?
src.explanation: Arousability separates the two states: sleep is unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by sensory or other stimuli, and coma is unconsciousness from which a person cannot be aroused. Failure to rouse to any stimulus points to coma.

items.html: Rapid eye movement sleep. Rapid eye movement sleep is the active, dreaming form of sleep: dreams are vivid, heart and breathing rates become irregular, and muscle tone is very depressed, with atonia of voluntary muscles except the eyes and diaphragm.
cites: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 9, 10, 14, 27, 28

src.question: Which state combines vivid dreaming, irregular heart and breathing rates, and very depressed muscle tone?
src.explanation: Rapid eye movement sleep is the active, dreaming form of sleep: dreams are vivid, heart and breathing rates become irregular, and muscle tone is very depressed, with atonia of voluntary muscles except the eyes and diaphragm.

items.section_title: 1.8 · EEG changes across wakefulness and sleep
items.html: Rapid eye movement sleep versus wakefulness. In rapid eye movement sleep the waves are irregular and high in frequency, beta waves like those of an awake, active person, which makes it often difficult to tell rapid eye movement sleep from alert wakefulness. Atonia of voluntary muscles is the difference.
cites: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 22, 25, 26, 28, 29

src.question: What shared electroencephalogram pattern makes rapid eye movement sleep hard to tell from alert wakefulness?
src.explanation: In rapid eye movement sleep the waves are irregular and high in frequency, beta waves like those of an awake, active person, which makes it often difficult to tell rapid eye movement sleep from alert wakefulness. Atonia of voluntary muscles is the difference.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Slow-wave (non-rapid eye movement) sleep, and the comparison
items.html: Non-rapid versus rapid eye movement physiology. Non-rapid eye movement sleep brings increased parasympathetic tone with low blood pressure, a slow heart rate and a decreased breathing rate, part of a 10 to 30% fall in vegetative functions. In rapid eye movement sleep, heart and breathing rates become irregular instead.
cites: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 10, 12, 14, 28

src.question: Which combination fits non-rapid eye movement sleep rather than rapid eye movement sleep?
src.key: Low blood pressure, slow heart rate
src.explanation: Non-rapid eye movement sleep brings increased parasympathetic tone with low blood pressure, a slow heart rate and a decreased breathing rate, part of a 10 to 30% fall in vegetative functions. In rapid eye movement sleep, heart and breathing rates become irregular instead.

items.html: Desynchronized sleep. Rapid eye movement sleep is also called desynchronized sleep because there is a lack of synchrony in neuron firing when there is brain activity. The tracing is irregular and high frequency, much like an awake, active person's.
cites: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 29, 22, 19

src.question: A 32-year-old woman's recording during a period of rapid eye movements shows irregular, high-frequency waves, and the technician labels it desynchronized sleep. What does that label describe?
src.explanation: Rapid eye movement sleep is also called desynchronized sleep because there is a lack of synchrony in neuron firing when there is brain activity. The tracing is irregular and high frequency, much like an awake, active person's, which fits her period of rapid eye movements.

items.html: Waking from rapid eye movement sleep. Rapid eye movement sleep is associated with vivid dreaming, and people can awaken spontaneously in the morning during rapid eye movement sleep; in a typical night the last rapid eye movement period leads into waking.
cites: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 9, 10, 13, 14, 7, 28

src.question: A 28-year-old woman wakes on her own at the end of a full night's sleep, recalling a vivid dream. From which sleep stage did she probably wake?
src.explanation: Rapid eye movement sleep is associated with vivid dreaming, and people can awaken spontaneously in the morning during rapid eye movement sleep; in a typical night the last rapid eye movement period leads into waking. Her spontaneous morning waking and vivid dream both point here.

items.html: Telling sleep from coma by arousal. Sleep is unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by sensory or other stimuli; coma is unconsciousness from which a person cannot be aroused. Waking when shaken shows he was arousable, so he was asleep, even though a quieter stimulus had failed first.
cites: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 5

src.question: A 20-year-old college student is slumped over a library desk with his eyes closed. A friend says his name quietly and he does not respond, but when the friend shakes his arm he wakes and starts talking. Which finding shows he was asleep rather than in a coma?
src.key: He woke when his arm was shaken
src.explanation: Sleep is unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by sensory or other stimuli; coma is unconsciousness from which a person cannot be aroused. Waking when his arm was shaken shows he was arousable, so he was asleep, even though a quieter stimulus had failed first.

items.html: Arousable unresponsiveness is sleep. A person who is unconscious yet is roused by a loud voice and a squeeze of the shoulder, and then answers questions, was asleep. Sleep is unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by sensory or other stimuli.
cites: CMS 1 Phases of Sleep - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 5, 27, 28

src.question: A 68-year-old man on a medical ward is found late at night lying still with his eyes closed, not answering when the nurse enters the room. When she calls his name loudly and squeezes his shoulder, he opens his eyes and answers her questions. Which state best explains his earlier unresponsiveness?
src.explanation: He was unconscious, yet a loud voice and a squeeze of the shoulder roused him and he answered questions. Sleep is unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by sensory or other stimuli, which is exactly what happened at his bedside.

items.section_title: 2.8 · The syllabus complications and comorbidities, one by one
items.html: Pulmonary hypertension in obstructive sleep apnea. Obstructive sleep apnea is classified with group 3 pulmonary hypertension, especially when it coexists with obesity hypoventilation syndrome or another cause of daytime hypoxemia. Right-sided heart failure from pulmonary hypertension is a late feature of obesity hypoventilation.
cites: CMS I Obstructive Sleep Apnea & Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 11, 19, 20, 30

src.question: Pulmonary hypertension from obstructive sleep apnea is especially likely when the apnea coexists with which condition?
src.explanation: Obstructive sleep apnea is classified with group 3 pulmonary hypertension, especially when it coexists with obesity hypoventilation syndrome or another cause of daytime hypoxemia. Right-sided heart failure from pulmonary hypertension is a late feature of obesity hypoventilation.

items.section_title: 2.2 · Obstructive sleep apnea: who gets it and why
items.html: Enlarged tonsils. Enlarged tonsils are a risk factor and examination finding of obstructive sleep apnea, alongside obesity, macroglossia, micrognathia, retrognathia, a thick neck and a crowded posterior oropharynx. They point to structural narrowing of the upper airway.
cites: CMS I Obstructive Sleep Apnea & Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 6, 7, 31

src.question: Which examination finding is a risk factor for obstructive sleep apnea rather than a screening feature for obesity hypoventilation syndrome?
src.explanation: Enlarged tonsils are a risk factor and examination finding of obstructive sleep apnea, alongside obesity, macroglossia, micrognathia, retrognathia, a thick neck and a crowded posterior oropharynx. They point to structural narrowing of the upper airway.

items.html: STOP-Bang worked total (4 and 3). Snoring 1 + observed apnea 1 + body mass index above 35 1 + neck 16 inches or larger 1 = 4; tiredness, pressure, age and gender (female) score 0. A total of 4 is intermediate, but yes to 2 of the first four questions plus a body mass index above 35 makes high risk. Snoring 1 + pressure 1 + age older than 50 1 = 3 is intermediate risk, and no combination rule applies.
cites: CMS I Obstructive Sleep Apnea & Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17

src.question: A woman answers yes to loud snoring and to being observed to stop breathing during sleep; her body mass index is 38 kg/m2 and her shirt collar is 16 inches. She is not tired during the day, is not treated for high blood pressure and is not older than 50. What is her STOP-Bang (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure, body mass index, age, neck, gender) total?
src.explanation: Snoring 1 + observed apnea 1 + body mass index above 35 1 + neck 16 inches or larger 1 = 4; tiredness, pressure, age and gender (female) score 0. A total of 4 is intermediate, but yes to 2 of the first four questions plus a body mass index above 35 makes her high risk.

also.explanation: Snoring 1 + pressure 1 + age older than 50 1 = 3; tiredness, observed apnea, body mass index (33 is not above 35), neck (15 is under 16 inches) and gender (female) score 0. A total of 3 is intermediate risk, and no combination rule applies.

items.html: Workup of obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion: alternative causes of hypercapnia and hypoventilation must be excluded. The workup therefore includes a metabolic panel, blood count, thyroid function tests, pulmonary function tests, chest radiograph and toxicology screen.
cites: CMS I Obstructive Sleep Apnea & Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 8, 32, 33

src.question: Why does the workup for obesity hypoventilation syndrome include a toxicology screen and thyroid function tests?
src.explanation: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion: alternative causes of hypercapnia and hypoventilation must be excluded. The workup therefore includes a metabolic panel, blood count, thyroid function tests, pulmonary function tests, chest radiograph and toxicology screen.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Obstructive sleep apnea: management, education and referral
items.html: Modafinil and armodafinil cautions. These stimulants need caution in patients with cardiovascular, hepatic or psychiatric conditions, so liver disease calls for care. They also have many potential drug interactions, and elderly patients receive lower doses.
cites: CMS I Obstructive Sleep Apnea & Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 6, 8, 11, 12

src.question: In which patient are modafinil and armodafinil used with caution?
src.explanation: These stimulants need caution in patients with cardiovascular, hepatic or psychiatric conditions, so liver disease calls for care. They also have many potential drug interactions, and elderly patients receive lower doses.

items.html: Obesity criterion. Obesity for this diagnosis means a body mass index above 30 kg/m2, together with awake arterial carbon dioxide above 45 mmHg and exclusion of other causes. The syndrome becomes more likely as body mass index increases, and patients are typically obese and hypersomnolent.
cites: CMS I Obstructive Sleep Apnea & Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slides 17, 28, 30, 32

src.question: What body mass index meets the obesity criterion for obesity hypoventilation syndrome?
src.explanation: Obesity for this diagnosis means a body mass index above 30, together with awake arterial carbon dioxide above 45 mmHg and exclusion of other causes. The syndrome becomes more likely as body mass index increases, and patients are typically obese and hypersomnolent.

items.html: High risk despite a total below 5. Snoring and tiredness are 2 of the first four questions, and a neck of 16 inches (40 cm) or larger completes a high-risk combination. The total is only 3, yet the person is high risk, as with 2 or more of the first four plus male gender or a body mass index above 35.
cites: CMS I Obstructive Sleep Apnea & Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome - Shah Fallsv.pptx, Slide 17

src.question: On the STOP-Bang (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure, body mass index, age, neck, gender) questionnaire, which set of yes answers places a person at high risk despite a total below 5?

items.html: STOP-Bang risk bands. items.html: Light’s criteria worked example: a transudate from cirrhosis. Protein ratio 1.2 / 5.8 = 0.21 (pleural fluid over serum), lactate dehydrogenase ratio 70 / 180 = 0.39, and fluid lactate dehydrogenase 70 is under two-thirds of 280 (the top of the normal 140-280 units/L), about 187: all of Light’s criteria are absent, a transudate. items.html: Stage 2B with a same-side hilar node. A tumor no more than 5 cm that has spread to the peribronchial, hilar or intrapulmonary nodes is stage 2B. A 2.8-cm tumor would be stage 1A without nodes, but an involved same-side hilar node, scored N1, moves it to stage 2B; mediastinal nodes would have made it stage 3.

src.question: A 64-year-old woman has a biopsy-proven 2.8-cm non-small cell carcinoma in the right upper lobe. Positron emission tomography shows uptake in a hilar lymph node on the same side, but no mediastinal or other nodes are involved, and there is no distant metastasis. Which stage is her cancer?
src.explanation: Correct. A tumor no more than 5 cm that has spread to the peribronchial, hilar or intrapulmonary nodes is stage 2B. Her 2.8-cm tumor would be stage 1A without nodes, but the involved same-side hilar node, scored N1, moves it to stage 2B; mediastinal nodes would have made it stage 3.

src.question: A 2 cm lung cancer has spread to mediastinal lymph nodes on the same side, with no distant metastasis; which stage is it?

also.explanation: Correct. Mediastinal or subcarinal node involvement (N2) automatically moves a cancer to stage 3, and a tumor no more than 5 cm that has spread to the mediastinal and subcarinal nodes is stage 3A. His tumor is only 2.5 cm, but the same-side mediastinal nodes set the stage.

items.section_title: 5.8 · Staging: TNM and the stage pictures
items.html: Stage 2A by size alone. Stage 2A is a tumor more than 4 cm but no more than 5 cm in its greatest dimension that has not spread to any lymph nodes. A 4.5 cm node-negative tumor without metastasis fits exactly, T2b N0 M0.

src.question: A 4.5 cm lung cancer has not spread to any lymph nodes or distant sites; which stage is it?
src.explanation: Correct. Stage 2A is a tumor more than 4 cm but no more than 5 cm in its greatest dimension that has not spread to any lymph nodes. A 4.5 cm node-negative tumor without metastasis fits exactly, T2b N0 M0.

Estrogen use fails the rule.

src.question: Which finding makes a patient fail the PERC (Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria)?
src.explanation: Correct. All eight PERC (Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria) items must be true to stop the workup: age under 50, heart rate under 100, oxygen saturation above 94%, no hemoptysis, no exogenous estrogen, no prior venous thromboembolism, no surgery or trauma and no unilateral leg swelling. items.html: Signs that a hypertrophied right ventricle has decompensated. When a chronically hypertrophied right ventricle decompensates, its elevated diastolic pressure transmits backward: the liver congests and becomes tender, ascites forms and pitting edema spreads in dependent areas.
cites: Pulmonary Vascular Disorders 2026 - Gray.pptx, Slide 11

src.question: A 72-year-old man has had interstitial lung disease for 8 years, and his right ventricle has been known to be hypertrophied. Over the past month his exertional dyspnea has worsened. Which new finding shows that his right ventricle has decompensated?
src.explanation: Correct. When a chronically hypertrophied right ventricle decompensates, its elevated diastolic pressure transmits backward: the liver congests and becomes tender, ascites forms and pitting edema spreads in dependent areas. A right ventricular heave, an intensified P2 and a tricuspid regurgitation murmur go with it.

items.html: A Wells score of 4.5 makes embolism likely. The rule-out criteria come after the Wells score and are used when it is 4 or less. A score of 4.5 makes embolism likely, so the D-dimer and the rule-out criteria are bypassed: directly to computed tomographic pulmonary angiography.
cites: Pulmonary Vascular Disorders 2026 - Gray.pptx, Slides 53, 57

src.question: A 38-year-old woman has been bedbound at home for 7 days with severe influenza and now has sudden dyspnea. The clinician judges pulmonary embolism more likely than any alternative diagnosis, giving a Wells score of 4.5. Her heart rate is 92/min and oxygen saturation 97%, and she has no hemoptysis, no estrogen use, no prior clots, no surgery or trauma and no leg swelling, so she would meet every PERC (Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria) item. Her kidney function is normal and she has no contrast allergy. Which step fits?
src.explanation: Correct. The rule-out criteria come after the Wells score and are used when it is 4 or less. Her score of 4.5 (embolism more likely than alternatives 3 + immobilization for more than 3 days 1.5) makes embolism likely, so the D-dimer and the rule-out criteria are bypassed and she goes directly to computed tomographic pulmonary angiography.

items.html: Wells points: heart rate above 100 = 1.5, hemoptysis = 1. Estrogen use is a risk factor and a PERC (Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria) item, but it is not on the Wells list. A score of 4 or less means embolism is unlikely.
cites: Pulmonary Vascular Disorders 2026 - Gray.pptx, Slides 53, 54

src.question: A 34-year-old woman who takes an estrogen-containing oral contraceptive has had 1 day of pleuritic chest pain and has coughed up a small amount of blood once. Her heart rate is 106/min and oxygen saturation 98%. Her legs show no swelling or tenderness, she has had no surgery or immobilization, she has had no previous clots and has no cancer, and the clinician judges viral pleurisy more likely than pulmonary embolism. What is her Wells score?
src.explanation: Correct. Heart rate above 100 (106/min) 1.5 + hemoptysis 1 + signs of deep vein thrombosis 0 + embolism more likely than alternatives 0 + surgery or immobilization 0 + previous clot 0 + malignancy 0 = 2.5. Estrogen use is a risk factor and a PERC (Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria) item, but it is not on the Wells list. A score of 4 or less means embolism is unlikely.

items.html: Acidosis shifts potassium out of cells. In acidosis hydrogen ions shift from the extracellular fluid into the cells, and potassium shifts out of cells into the extracellular fluid. The potassium that moves out raises the serum potassium, resulting in hyperkalemia.

src.question: In acidosis, which shift explains the hyperkalemia?
src.key: Hydrogen enters cells as potassium leaves
src.explanation: In acidosis hydrogen ions shift from the extracellular fluid into the cells, and potassium shifts from inside the cells out to the extracellular fluid. The potassium that moves out raises the serum level, resulting in hyperkalemia.

also.key: Potassium moves out of cells, raising serum potassium
also.explanation: A 47-year-old man is admitted after a crush injury with prolonged poor tissue perfusion. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.31 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 29 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which change should be expected from his acid-base disturbance itself? A pH of 7.31 with a bicarbonate of 14 is a metabolic acidosis (poor perfusion and trauma cause lactic acidosis). In acidosis, hydrogen ions shift into cells and potassium shifts out of cells into the extracellular fluid, resulting in hyperkalemia.

items.html: Alkalosis shifts potassium into cells. In alkalosis hydrogen ions shift from inside the cells out to the extracellular fluid, and potassium shifts the other way, from the extracellular fluid into the cells. The serum potassium falls, so alkalosis results in hypokalemia, with no potassium actually lost from the body.
cites: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slide 5
PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 5, 39

src.question: In alkalosis, which way does potassium shift, and what serum level results?
src.explanation: In alkalosis hydrogen ions shift from inside the cells out to the extracellular fluid, and potassium shifts the other way, from the extracellular fluid into the cells. The serum potassium falls, so alkalosis results in hypokalemia.

also.key: Potassium shifted into cells as hydrogen ions left them
also.explanation: A 31-year-old woman has been breathing rapidly for 30 minutes during a panic attack. She has not vomited, has no diarrhea and takes no medicines. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.54 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 28 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 23 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Her potassium is 3.3 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L). Which process best accounts for her potassium level? A pH of 7.54 with a carbon dioxide of 28 is a respiratory alkalosis from anxiety. In alkalosis hydrogen ions shift out of cells and potassium shifts into cells, resulting in hypokalemia, with no potassium actually lost from the body.

items.html: Acid-base and oxygen delivery. In acidosis hemoglobin has a decreased affinity for oxygen, so it gives oxygen up more readily and oxygen delivery to the tissues increases. Alkalosis does the reverse: it increases hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, so less oxygen is delivered to the tissues.
cites: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slide 5

src.question: In acidosis, how does hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen change, and what happens to tissue oxygen delivery?
src.explanation: In acidosis hemoglobin has a decreased affinity for oxygen, so it gives oxygen up more readily and oxygen delivery to the tissues increases. Alkalosis does the reverse: higher affinity and less delivery to the tissues.

also.key: Higher hemoglobin affinity; less oxygen delivered
also.explanation: A 29-year-old woman has vomited repeatedly for 3 days. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.48 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 47 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 34 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which effect on oxygen delivery does her acid-base disorder produce? A pH of 7.48 with a bicarbonate of 34 is a metabolic alkalosis (vomiting loses gastric acid), and the carbon dioxide of 47 is respiratory compensation. Alkalosis increases hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, so less oxygen is delivered to the tissues.

items.section_title: 7.2 · Normal values and the anion gap (objective f)
items.html: What raises the anion gap. The anion gap increases with more unmeasured anions, such as anionic proteins (albumin), ketoacids, phosphate and lactate, or with fewer unmeasured cations such as calcium, magnesium and potassium.
cites: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slide 7

src.question: Which change raises the anion gap?
src.explanation: The anion gap increases with more unmeasured anions, such as anionic proteins (albumin), ketoacids, phosphate and lactate, or with fewer unmeasured cations such as calcium, magnesium and potassium. Ketoacids are unmeasured anions, so they widen the gap.

items.section_title: 7.2 · Normal values and the anion gap (objective f)
items.html: Lithium lowers the gap. A decreased gap, below the normal 6 to 12, comes from added abnormal cations such as lithium, which are not counted in the formula.
cites: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 7, 48

src.question: A 41-year-old woman has bipolar disorder treated with lithium and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. Routine testing shows sodium 136 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 106 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 26 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L), albumin 4.4 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL), and no monoclonal protein. Which part of her history best accounts for her anion gap?
src.explanation: Her gap is 136 - (26 + 106) = 4, below the normal 6 to 12. A decreased gap comes from added abnormal cations such as lithium, which are not counted in the formula. Her normal albumin and absent monoclonal protein remove the other low-gap causes.

items.section_title: 7.2 · Normal values and the anion gap (objective f)
items.html: Calculate the gap; do not assume it. The anion gap can be abnormal even when sodium, chloride and bicarbonate are each within the normal range, so it has to be calculated rather than assumed.
cites: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 8, 26

src.question: A chemistry panel shows sodium, chloride and bicarbonate each within its normal range. What follows for the anion gap?
src.explanation: The anion gap can be abnormal even when sodium, chloride and bicarbonate are each within the normal range, so it has to be calculated rather than assumed. That is why calculating the gap is its own step after the primary disorder is identified.

items.section_title: 7.2 · Normal values and the anion gap (objective f)
items.html: Anion gap formula. Anion gap = sodium - (bicarbonate + chloride), for example 138 - (14 + 103) = 21, above the normal 6 to 12. A raised gap with a low pH and low bicarbonate is a raised-gap metabolic acidosis, and renal failure is on that list.
cites: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 7, 26, 45

src.question: A 54-year-old man with chronic kidney failure has fatigue. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.29 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 30 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 103 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L), potassium 4.0 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L). What is his anion gap?
src.explanation: Anion gap = sodium - (bicarbonate + chloride) = 138 - (14 + 103) = 138 - 117 = 21, above the normal 6 to 12. A raised gap with a low pH and low bicarbonate is a raised-gap metabolic acidosis, and renal failure is on that list.

items.section_title: 7.2 · Normal values and the anion gap (objective f)
items.html: Correcting the gap for albumin. The gap must be corrected when albumin is abnormal: the correction adds 2.5 for each 1 g/dL that albumin sits below 4.5. Albumin 2.5 g/dL is 2 below 4.5, so the correction adds 2 x 2.5 = 5, and a measured gap of 12 becomes a corrected gap of 17, above the normal 6 to 12. A gap that looks normal can be a raised gap once corrected.

src.question: A 63-year-old woman with months of poor oral intake is admitted with a new infection. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.33 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 35 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 18 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 136 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 106 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 18 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Her albumin is 2.5 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL). What is her anion gap after correction for her albumin?
src.explanation: The measured gap is 136 - (18 + 106) = 12. The correction adds 2.5 for each 1 g/dL that albumin sits below 4.5: 4.5 - 2.5 = 2, and 2 x 2.5 = 5, so the corrected gap is 12 + 5 = 17, above the normal 6 to 12.

also.explanation: A 64-year-old woman with cirrhosis takes a diuretic and has a serum albumin 2.1 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL). Arterial blood gas: pH 7.53 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 37 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 30 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 134 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 93 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). What is her anion gap corrected for albumin? Gap = 134 - (93 + 30) = 11. Albumin is 4.5 - 2.1 = 2.4 g/dL below 4.5, so add 2.5 x 2.4 = 6. Corrected gap = 11 + 6 = 17, above 6 to 12: a raised-gap acidosis is hidden under her metabolic alkalosis.

A 76-year-old woman with long-standing poor nutrition becomes confused with a low blood pressure and cool extremities. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.34 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 36 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 19 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 137 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 106 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 19 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Her albumin is 2.1 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL). Which acid-base disorder do her results show? Low pH and low bicarbonate make a metabolic acidosis. The measured gap is 137 - (19 + 106) = 12, but her albumin is 2.4 g/dL below 4.5, adding 2.4 x 2.5 = 6, so the corrected gap is 18, above 12. Poor perfusion causes lactic acidosis, a raised-gap cause.

also.key: Correct the anion gap for albumin
also.explanation: A 63-year-old woman with cirrhosis has an infection and low blood pressure; her serum albumin 1.9 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL). Arterial blood gas: pH 7.34 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 31 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 16 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 133 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 105 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Her gap is 12 and her carbon dioxide fits the predicted compensation. Which step should come next? Her gap = 133 - (105 + 16) = 12 looks normal, but albumin 1.9 is 2.6 below 4.5, so the corrected gap = 12 + 2.5 x 2.6 = 18.5, raised. The gap must be corrected when albumin is abnormal, and doing so changes her diagnosis to a raised-gap acidosis.

src.explanation: The pH comes first: below 7.35 is acidemia and above 7.45 is alkalemia. Only then are the carbon dioxide and bicarbonate checked to see which one matches the pH direction, naming the disorder respiratory or metabolic.

items.html: Volatile acid leaves through the lungs. Volatile acids from fats and carbohydrates, carbonic acid, are eliminated by the lungs as carbon dioxide. Nonvolatile acids from proteins and ingested sulfates and phosphates are eliminated by the kidneys.

src.question: Carbonic acid, the volatile acid made from fat and carbohydrate metabolism, is eliminated by which organ?
src.explanation: Volatile acids from fats and carbohydrates, carbonic acid, are eliminated by the lungs as carbon dioxide. Nonvolatile acids from proteins and ingested sulfates and phosphates are eliminated by the kidneys.

items.html: Compensation never fully corrects the pH. In a simple disorder the compensatory response moves the pH toward normal but will not fully correct the pH disturbance; the underlying condition must be corrected to restore pH balance. A normal pH beside an abnormal carbon dioxide and bicarbonate therefore points to a mixed disorder rather than to no abnormality.

src.question: In a simple acid-base disorder, what does compensation do to the pH?
src.key: Moves it toward normal, not fully
src.explanation: The compensatory response will not fully correct the pH disturbance in a simple disorder; the underlying condition must be corrected to restore pH balance. A normal pH with abnormal values therefore raises the question of a mixed disorder.

also.explanation: In a simple acid-base disorder, how far does compensation move the pH? The compensatory response will not fully correct the pH disturbance; the underlying condition must be corrected to restore pH balance. A pH sitting right on normal therefore raises the question of a second, opposing disorder.

also.key: It moves pH toward normal without fully correcting it
also.explanation: A 72-year-old woman has chronic respiratory acidosis from long-standing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.33 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 68 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 35 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). A student predicts her kidneys will bring her pH back to 7.40 with time. Which statement about her compensation is accurate? Compensation will not fully correct the pH disturbance; the underlying condition must be corrected to restore balance. Her kidneys have raised the bicarbonate to 35, which pulls the pH up toward normal, but it remains 7.33.

An arterial blood gas shows pH 7.40 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 60 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 36 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What does the normal pH indicate? Both the carbon dioxide of 60 and the bicarbonate of 36 are abnormal, yet the pH is 7.40. Compensation does not fully correct the pH in a simple disorder, so a normal pH beside abnormal values points to a mixed disorder rather than to no abnormality.

items.html: Renal compensation of respiratory acidosis. A primary respiratory acidosis is compensated by the kidneys, which retain bicarbonate over hours to days. When chronic, bicarbonate is expected to rise 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in carbon dioxide, from baselines of 40 mm Hg and 25 mEq/L.
cites: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 19, 23, 24, 34

src.question: A 68-year-old man has had obesity hypoventilation syndrome for many years. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.33 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 66 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 34 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). For respiratory acidosis, bicarbonate is expected to rise 1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in carbon dioxide when acute and 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg when chronic, from baselines of 40 mm Hg and 25 mEq/L. Which process accounts for his bicarbonate of 34?
src.key: The kidneys retaining bicarbonate over days
src.explanation: A primary respiratory acidosis is compensated by the kidneys, which retain bicarbonate over hours to days. A chronic rise of 26 mm Hg predicts 25 + 3.5 x 2.6 = about 34, exactly his value, so this is the expected renal compensation.

items.html: Compensation for metabolic acidosis is respiratory. Metabolic acidosis is an excess of acid to buffer or a net loss of bicarbonate. Respiration increases to decrease carbon dioxide, seen as compensatory hyperventilation and, when severe, Kussmaul breathing.
cites: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 5, 41, 42

src.question: How does the body compensate for metabolic acidosis?
src.key: Breathing more to lower carbon dioxide
src.explanation: Metabolic acidosis is an excess of acid to buffer or a net loss of bicarbonate. Compensation is respiratory: respiration increases to decrease carbon dioxide, seen as compensatory hyperventilation and, when severe, Kussmaul breathing.

items.section_title: 7.7 · Approach to the patient and mixed disorders (objectives d, e, f)
items.html: Chronic respiratory acidosis with a concurrent metabolic alkalosis. In chronic respiratory acidosis bicarbonate rises 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in carbon dioxide from a baseline of 40 mm Hg and 25 mEq/L, so a carbon dioxide of 60 predicts 25 + 3.5 x (60 - 40) / 10 = 32. A bicarbonate above the prediction, such as 37, means something beyond the kidneys is adding bicarbonate (loss of gastric acid by suction, or a diuretic): a concurrent metabolic alkalosis. Discontinuing contributors such as diuretics and treating potassium deficits are the listed steps for metabolic alkalosis.
cites: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 23, 29, 34, 54
PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 29, 34, 37, 54

src.question: A 67-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has had nasogastric suction for 3 days after bowel surgery. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.41 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 60 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 37 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). From a baseline carbon dioxide of 40 mm Hg and bicarbonate of 25 mEq/L, in chronic respiratory acidosis bicarbonate rises 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in carbon dioxide. What does his bicarbonate indicate?
src.explanation: Chronic compensation predicts bicarbonate = 25 + 3.5 x (60 - 40) / 10 = 25 + 7 = 32. His is 37, 5 above prediction, so something beyond the kidneys is adding bicarbonate: loss of gastric acid by suction. A normal pH with a high carbon dioxide also signals a mixed disorder.

also.key: Stop the diuretic and replace potassium
also.explanation: A 73-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease takes a diuretic and has a potassium of 3.1 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L). Arterial blood gas: pH 7.42 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 61 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 38 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 137 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 88 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). From a baseline carbon dioxide of 40 mm Hg and bicarbonate of 25 mEq/L, in chronic respiratory acidosis bicarbonate rises 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in carbon dioxide. Which is the most appropriate management? Chronic compensation predicts bicarbonate = 25 + 3.5 x 2.1 = about 32; hers is 38, a metabolic alkalosis on top of chronic respiratory acidosis. Discontinuing contributors such as diuretics and treating potassium deficits are the listed steps for metabolic alkalosis.

items.html: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease treated with diuretics. The classic metabolic alkalosis plus respiratory acidosis: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is a listed cause of respiratory acidosis, and diuretics cause a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis. The carbon dioxide is higher than predicted and the pH can be normal.

src.question: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease treated with diuretics is the classic example of which mixed disorder?
src.explanation: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is a listed cause of respiratory acidosis, and diuretics cause a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis. The carbon dioxide is higher than predicted and the pH can be normal.

items.section_title: 7.7 · Approach to the patient and mixed disorders (objectives d, e, f)
items.html: Sepsis: metabolic acidosis plus respiratory alkalosis. Lactic acidosis from sepsis is a raised-gap metabolic acidosis, and the prevailing carbon dioxide sits below the predicted value (expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x bicarbonate + 8): a concurrent respiratory alkalosis, which can bring the pH back to normal.

src.question: Lactic acidosis from sepsis in the intensive care unit is the classic example of which mixed disorder?
src.explanation: Lactic acidosis is a raised-gap metabolic acidosis, and in sepsis the prevailing carbon dioxide sits below the predicted value: a concurrent respiratory alkalosis. The pH can even look normal.

also.key: Raised-gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis
also.explanation: A 72-year-old malnourished woman from a nursing home has a urinary infection, hypotension and a respiratory rate of 30. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.44 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 26 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 17 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 134 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 105 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), albumin 1.7 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL). Which acid-base disorders are present? Gap = 134 - (105 + 17) = 12, which looks normal, but corrected gap = 12 + 2.5 x (4.5 - 1.7) = 12 + 7 = 19, raised. Expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x 17 + 8 = 33.5, range 31.5 to 35.5; her 26 is below it, a concurrent respiratory alkalosis, which brings the pH back to normal in sepsis.

items.html: Diarrhea with a respiratory depressant. A gap of 139 - (115 + 14) = 10 is normal, with a high chloride: the normal-gap acidosis of diarrhea. Expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x 14 + 8 = 29, range 27 to 31; a carbon dioxide of 36 is above it, a concurrent respiratory acidosis from the respiratory depressant.

src.question: A 59-year-old man with 5 days of diarrhea was given a benzodiazepine overnight for agitation and is now drowsy with slow, shallow breathing. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.21 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 36 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 139 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 115 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorders are present?
src.key: Normal-gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory acidosis
src.explanation: Gap = 139 - (115 + 14) = 10, normal, with a high chloride: the normal-gap acidosis of diarrhea. Expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x 14 + 8 = 29, range 27 to 31; his 36 is above it, a concurrent respiratory acidosis from the respiratory depressant.

items.html: Change in anion gap against change in bicarbonate. Change in anion gap = calculated anion gap minus a normal gap, with 10 the accepted value (using the gap corrected for albumin when albumin is low). It is compared with the change in bicarbonate, measured from an accepted normal of 25; the two should be equal in a simple metabolic acidosis. A gap change larger than the bicarbonate change points to a concurrent metabolic alkalosis, such as from vomiting, holding bicarbonate up.

src.question: How is the change in anion gap calculated?
src.explanation: Change in anion gap = calculated anion gap minus a normal gap, with 10 the accepted value. It is then compared with the change in bicarbonate, measured from an accepted normal of 25; the two should be equal in a simple metabolic acidosis.

also.explanation: A metabolic acidosis has sodium 140 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 100 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What is the change in anion gap? Anion gap 140 - (14 + 100) = 26. Change in gap = calculated gap - 10 = 16. The change in bicarbonate is 25 - 14 = 11, so the gap change is the larger of the two; a gap change larger than the bicarbonate change points to a concurrent metabolic alkalosis.

A 71-year-old man with kidney failure has vomited for 3 days. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.39 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 39 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 23 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 92 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Using 10 as the normal anion gap, what is his change in anion gap? Gap = 138 - (92 + 23) = 23. Change in gap = 23 - 10 = 13. Against a change in bicarbonate of only 25 - 23 = 2, the gap rose far more, the sign of a metabolic alkalosis from vomiting on top of the uremic acidosis.

A 49-year-old man with alcoholic ketoacidosis has vomited repeatedly for 2 days. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.36 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 33 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 18 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 136 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 90 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Using 10 as the normal anion gap and 25 mEq/L as the normal bicarbonate, what does comparing the change in anion gap with the change in bicarbonate show? Gap = 136 - (90 + 18) = 28, change in gap = 18; change in bicarbonate = 25 - 18 = 7. The gap rose far more than the bicarbonate fell, so a metabolic alkalosis from vomiting is holding bicarbonate up, detectable here because the gap is high.

A 57-year-old woman with nephrotic syndrome and a urinary infection has a serum albumin 2.5 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL). Arterial blood gas: pH 7.36 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 37 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 20 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 104 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Using 10 as the normal anion gap and 25 mEq/L as the normal bicarbonate, what is her change in anion gap once the gap is corrected for albumin? Gap = 138 - (104 + 20) = 14. Albumin is 2 below 4.5, so add 2.5 x 2 = 5: corrected gap = 19. Change in gap = 19 - 10 = 9. Against a change in bicarbonate of 25 - 20 = 5, the gap rose more.

items.section_title: 7.7 · Approach to the patient and mixed disorders (objectives d, e, f)
items.html: Uremic acidosis with vomiting: treat both causes. A gap of 143 - (97 + 25) = 21, a change in gap of 11, with no change in bicarbonate is a uremic acidosis with a metabolic alkalosis from vomiting. Both causes need treatment: replace the fluid deficit for the vomiting and treat the uremia (the kidney failure).
cites: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 63, 30, 54, 23

src.question: A 68-year-old man with uremia from kidney failure has vomited for 5 days and is dry on examination. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.41 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 41 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 25 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 143 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 97 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Using 10 as the normal anion gap and 25 mEq/L as the normal bicarbonate, which treatment approach is most appropriate?
src.key: Replace fluids and treat the kidney failure
src.explanation: Gap = 143 - (97 + 25) = 21, change in gap = 11, change in bicarbonate = 0: a uremic acidosis with a metabolic alkalosis from vomiting. Both causes need treatment: replace his fluid deficit for the vomiting and treat the uremia.

items.html: Raised-gap plus normal-gap metabolic acidosis. When the bicarbonate fell more than the gap rose, and the change in bicarbonate is accounted for by the change in gap and a rise in chloride together, a raised-gap and a normal-gap metabolic acidosis are present at once, as in diarrhea with lactic acidosis, or a clearing diabetic ketoacidosis treated with saline.

src.question: In a raised-gap acidosis, the change in bicarbonate is larger than the change in anion gap, and it equals the change in anion gap plus a rise in chloride. What does this show?
src.explanation: When the change in bicarbonate is accounted for by the change in gap and the change in chloride together, a raised-gap and a normal-gap metabolic acidosis are present at once, as in diarrhea with lactic acidosis.

also.explanation: A 31-year-old woman has been treated for diabetic ketoacidosis with saline and insulin for 10 hours; her ketones are clearing. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.28 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 24 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 11 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 141 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 112 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Using 10 as the normal anion gap and 25 mEq/L as the normal bicarbonate, which acid-base disorders are present? Gap = 141 - (112 + 11) = 18, change in gap = 8; change in bicarbonate = 25 - 11 = 14. The bicarbonate fell more than the gap rose, and her chloride of 112 is high, so a normal-gap acidosis has joined the clearing ketoacidosis, the pattern listed for treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis.

A 54-year-old woman has had profuse watery diarrhea for 6 days and is now hypotensive with cool extremities and a high lactate. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.22 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 20 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 8 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 110 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Using 10 as the normal anion gap and 25 mEq/L as the normal bicarbonate, which acid-base disorders are present? Gap = 138 - (110 + 8) = 20, change in gap = 10; change in bicarbonate = 25 - 8 = 17. The bicarbonate fell more than the gap rose, and the high chloride of 110 accounts for the rest: lactic acidosis plus the normal-gap acidosis of diarrhea. Carbon dioxide 20 sits in the predicted 18 to 22 (1.5 x 8 + 8).

items.section_title: 7.7 · Approach to the patient and mixed disorders (objectives d, e, f)
items.html: Acute respiratory acidosis with a concurrent metabolic acidosis. Acute compensation predicts bicarbonate = 25 + 1 x (70 - 40) / 10 = 28 for a carbon dioxide of 70. A bicarbonate far below it (19) with a raised gap of 22 means a lactic acidosis from blood loss has joined the respiratory acidosis, driving the pH to 7.06.
cites: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 23, 24, 32, 33, 45

src.question: A 63-year-old man has a flail chest (a segment of chest wall moving inward on inspiration) and is bleeding into his abdomen after a car crash. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.06 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 70 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 19 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 139 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 98 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). From a baseline carbon dioxide of 40 mm Hg and bicarbonate of 25 mEq/L, in acute respiratory acidosis bicarbonate rises 1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in carbon dioxide. Is a second disorder present?
src.explanation: Acute compensation predicts bicarbonate = 25 + 1 x (70 - 40) / 10 = 28. His is 19, far below, and his gap = 139 - (98 + 19) = 22 is raised: a lactic acidosis from blood loss joins the respiratory acidosis of his flail chest, driving the pH to 7.06.

items.html: Severe respiratory acidosis: secure ventilation. A carbon dioxide above 80 mm Hg with life-threatening hypoxia (partial pressure of oxygen below 40) is an acute, severe failure of carbon dioxide excretion. It needs adequate ventilation, which may mean an emergency airway and a mechanical ventilator, plus oxygen.

src.question: A 67-year-old man with severe pneumonia is increasingly somnolent. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.16 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 88 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 30 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). His partial pressure of oxygen is 36 mm Hg (normal 80 to 100 mm Hg). Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.key: Secure the airway and ventilate mechanically
src.explanation: A carbon dioxide above 80 mm Hg with life-threatening hypoxia (partial pressure of oxygen below 40) is an acute, severe failure of carbon dioxide excretion. He needs adequate ventilation, which may mean an emergency airway and a mechanical ventilator, plus oxygen.

items.html: Medicine review in respiratory acidosis. Treatment starts with the cause and a medicine review: stop respiratory depressants, narcotics and benzodiazepines, which reduce ventilation.
cites: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 32, 36

src.question: A 74-year-old woman is drowsy 2 days after hip surgery. She takes an opioid for pain, a benzodiazepine at night for anxiety, a thiazide for hypertension and an inhaled bronchodilator for asthma. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.26 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 62 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 27 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which of her medicines should be stopped?
src.explanation: Low pH with a high carbon dioxide and a bicarbonate only slightly raised is an acute respiratory acidosis. Treatment starts with the cause and a medicine review: stop respiratory depressants, narcotics and benzodiazepines, which reduce ventilation.

items.html: Chronic respiratory acidosis: avoid a rapid fall in carbon dioxide. Treatment is similar to acute disease but with careful oxygen, because a rapidly falling carbon dioxide in chronic respiratory acidosis may trigger the complications of alkalosis: cardiac arrhythmias, reduced cerebral perfusion and seizures.
cites: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 34, 36, 37

src.question: A 70-year-old man with long-standing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and chronic carbon dioxide retention has an exacerbation. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.32 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 74 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 37 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). His partial pressure of oxygen is 52 mm Hg (normal 80 to 100 mm Hg). Which approach should be avoided?
src.key: Driving his carbon dioxide down rapidly
src.explanation: His bicarbonate of 37 shows chronic renal compensation. Treatment is similar to acute disease but with careful oxygen, because a rapidly falling carbon dioxide in chronic respiratory acidosis may trigger the complications of alkalosis: cardiac arrhythmias, reduced cerebral perfusion and seizures.

items.html: Acute bicarbonate rise. In acute respiratory acidosis bicarbonate climbs 1 mEq/L for each 10 mm Hg rise in carbon dioxide (3.5 mEq/L when chronic). A rise from 40 to 70 mm Hg is three steps of 10, so a baseline bicarbonate of 24 rises by 3 to 27 mEq/L.
cites: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 24, 33, 34, 35

src.question: Carbon dioxide rises from 40 to 70 mm Hg within the past hour, from a baseline bicarbonate of 24 mEq/L. The acute bicarbonate rise is 1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg and the chronic rise is 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg. What bicarbonate is expected?
src.explanation: A rise within the past hour is acute, so bicarbonate climbs 1 mEq/L for each 10 mm Hg. Carbon dioxide rose 30 mm Hg, three steps of 10, so bicarbonate rises 3: 24 + 3 = 27 mEq/L.

items.html: Mild respiratory alkalosis: treat the driver. A mild pH alteration, a pH below 7.50, usually does not require treatment. Management targets the driver, such as pain, anxiety, fever, infection or salicylate overdose, with mindful breathing to help control hyperventilation.

PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 39, 40

src.question: Respiratory alkalosis with a pH below 7.50 usually calls for which treatment?
src.explanation: A mild pH alteration, a pH below 7.50, usually does not require treatment. Management targets the driver, such as pain, anxiety, fever, infection or salicylate overdose, with mindful breathing to help control hyperventilation.

also.key: Slow, mindful breathing can ease the episodes
also.explanation: A 26-year-old woman has episodes of rapid breathing and palpitations when she is anxious; her examination is otherwise normal. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.48 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 32 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 23 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which counseling point is most appropriate? A pH of 7.48 with a low carbon dioxide is a mild respiratory alkalosis from anxiety. With a pH below 7.50 treatment is usually not required; treating the anxiety and mindful breathing to control the hyperventilation are the measures.

items.html: Saline is a normal-gap cause. A metabolic acidosis with a normal gap, such as 140 - (15 + 115) = 10, and a high chloride fits saline infusion, a normal-gap cause, so further large-volume normal saline feeding the acidosis is the part to limit.
cites: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 45, 46, 53

src.question: A 55-year-old woman has received large volumes of normal saline for 3 days after abdominal surgery. She also takes acetaminophen for pain, has nasogastric suction, and takes a loop diuretic for edema. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.32 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 30 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 140 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 115 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which part of her care should be limited?
src.explanation: Low pH and bicarbonate make a metabolic acidosis, and the gap is 140 - (15 + 115) = 10, normal, with a high chloride. Saline infusion is a normal-gap cause, so the infusion feeding the acidosis is the part to limit.

src.question: A 72-year-old man has chronic kidney failure that has worsened over months, adrenal insufficiency on hormone replacement, glaucoma treated with an oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, and leg edema treated with a loop diuretic. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.32 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 30 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 103 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which part of his history best accounts for this blood gas?
src.explanation: Low pH and bicarbonate make a metabolic acidosis, and the gap is 138 - (15 + 103) = 20, above 12. Renal failure, acute or chronic, is one of the big four raised-gap causes. His other conditions do not raise the gap.

also.explanation: A 66-year-old man has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, hypertension treated with a thiazide, asthma treated with an inhaled bronchodilator, and kidney function that has worsened over a month. Serum ketones are negative. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.27 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 25 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 11 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 139 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 104 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 11 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which of his medicines should be stopped because it adds to this acidosis? Low pH with a bicarbonate of 11 is a metabolic acidosis, and the gap is 139 - (11 + 104) = 24, well above 12. Metformin is on the raised-gap list, and stopping possible contributors is part of treating the underlying cause.

A 77-year-old man with a urinary infection is hypotensive, with cool, mottled skin, and is breathing fast. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.43 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 22 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 139 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 101 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Which process best explains his raised anion gap? Gap = 139 - (101 + 14) = 24, a raised-gap acidosis. Lactic acidosis from poor tissue perfusion is one of the big four raised-gap causes and fits his hypotension and mottling. His carbon dioxide of 22 is below the predicted 27 to 31 (1.5 x 14 + 8 = 29, plus or minus 2), a concurrent respiratory alkalosis of sepsis.

items.html: Carbon dioxide above the Winter range: a concurrent respiratory acidosis. Winter formula: expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x bicarbonate + 8; with a bicarbonate of 12, 1.5 x 12 + 8 = 26, range 24 to 28. A measured carbon dioxide above that range, even a value below normal such as 34 or 36, is higher than compensation requires: a concurrent respiratory acidosis. Respiratory depressants such as narcotics (an opioid) and benzodiazepines cause decreased ventilation: stop them and treat the cause, such as the infection.
